extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and educational researchers studying undergraduate pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical, quasi-experimental study design and implementation guidelines for testing the effect of inquiry-based learning versus traditional lecture in a college algebra course. Covers pedagogical steps, instrumentation, data collection, statistical analysis, and validity/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-test
rubrics_metrics.description: This study used a quasi-experimental design, with pre- and post-test to determine the effect of the instructional pedagogy on mathematics academic achievement of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre- and post-intervention measures when random assignment is not possible; clearly document self-enrollment / convenience sampling and acknowledge limitations introduced by lack of random assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pre-test as covariate and ANCOVA analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of covariance results from 41 students revealed, when controlling for college algebra readiness pre-test scores, students in the inquiry-based learning section showed significantly higher mathematics achievement post-test scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ANCOVA with the pre-test as covariate to control for baseline differences; report adjusted means, standard errors, confidence intervals, F, p-values, and effect sizes (η2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check statistical assumptions (normality, homogeneity, linearity, homogeneity of regression slopes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statistical assumptions of normality, homogeneity of variance, and homogeneity of covariance were inspected and addressed. Shapiro-Wilk’s test indicated residuals deviated from normality; homogeneity of regression slopes was tested via the interaction of covariate and independent variable; Levene’s test used for homogeneity of variance; scatterplots checked linearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct assumption tests (e.g., Shapiro-Wilk, Levene's, interaction term for slopes, scatterplots for linearity) and report results. If assumptions are violated, use appropriate alternative analyses or robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative / non-parametric validation when assumptions violated
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to the violation of the normality assumption, a non-parametric procedure recommended by Conover (1999) was carried out: non-parametric ANCOVA using the ranked dependent variable and covariate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-validate parametric results with non-parametric procedures (e.g., rank-based ANCOVA) to ensure conclusions are robust to assumption violations; report parallel findings and effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and interpret effect sizes and significance with pre-specified alpha
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical significance was set at an a priori level of α = .05. ANCOVA results revealed the main effect of instructional pedagogy was statistically significant, F(1, 38)=20.70, p<.001, with a large effect size (η2=.35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set alpha a priori, report F, p, and effect size (η2) to convey magnitude; interpret significance alongside effect size rather than p-value alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument reliability and content validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The college algebra readiness pre-test and the mathematics achievement post-test were developed by the researcher. Reliability was assessed via test-retest (r = .997 and r = .998). Content validity was examined by three experienced faculty members who agreed the content matched objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reliability (e.g., test-retest) on a separate sample and obtain faculty/expert review for content validity. Report reliability coefficients and the process of expert validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control threats to internal validity and state mitigation steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Three primary potential threats: diffusion of treatment (participants communicating), testing effect (participants remember responses), and instrumentation threat (instrument changes). The instructor controlled these threats by not informing sections about each other, administering different exams before and after intervention, and using the same instrument for pre- and post-test eight weeks apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify likely internal validity threats for the chosen design and state concrete steps taken to mitigate each threat; document adherence to those controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe sample, demographics, group sizes, and attrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were 41 students (23 inquiry-based, 18 traditional). Demographic breakdowns (gender, age distribution, race/ethnicity, full-time status) were provided. Dropouts and reasons (e.g., inability to afford online homework software) were reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comprehensive participant descriptions, report initial intended sample, actual analyzed sample, reasons for attrition, and potential biases introduced by attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain parity of instructional materials across conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor used the same materials in both classes: same textbook (Essentials of college algebra with modeling and visualization) and same MyMathLab assignments; both sections had same homework and used graphic calculators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identical materials, homework, and resources across experimental and control sections where possible to isolate the effect of pedagogy; document any differences and their potential impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document instructor qualifications and training
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor had over 22 years of teaching experience, participated in an inquiry-based learning workshop, and had been teaching using inquiry-based learning for over two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report instructor experience, specific training in the intervention pedagogy, and prior implementation history to support fidelity and interpret instructor effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed, sequenced implementation steps for inquiry-based learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry-based section implemented a sequence: (1) instructor overview and demonstration, (2) form groups and select leader, (3) five minutes individual thinking, (4) instructor circulates listening, (5) instructor asks probing questions to uncover thinking, (6) instructor provides hints not answers, (7) repeat steps multiple times, (8) group leader writes detailed solution on whiteboard, (9) compare solutions, (10) groups present solutions to whole class and answer questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concrete, repeatable sequence of in-class activities that operationalize inquiry-based learning so others can replicate the intervention and check fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group composition, rotation, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry-based learning groups of three to four students were formed to be diverse in gender, academic ability, age, and year; leadership rotated so each member took a lead role, asked questions, provided feedback, reflected on solutions, and discussed errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form diverse small groups with rotating leadership to promote accountability, distributed responsibility, and equitable engagement; document group-formation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor role as facilitator using probing questions and scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor moved between groups, listened to discussions, asked students to explain strategies to uncover prior knowledge, inquired into students' thinking, fostered equity in design/facilitation, encouraged reflection, and provided hints rather than answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize facilitator behaviors (probing, listening, scaffolding, equity-focused facilitation) rather than content delivery; specify examples of probing prompts and non-directive hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-active learning procedures (individual thinking, collaboration, presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students were asked to think individually for five minutes before group work, then collaborate to process mathematical ideas, practice communication, and present solutions to the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that combine individual reflection, peer collaboration, and public presentation to develop conceptual understanding, communication, and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formative feedback and continuous assessment in inquiry-based learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry-based learning provides students with formative and continuous feedback that can help them understand their mistakes, improve their work, and better understand their thought process; instructors can adjust pedagogy accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor formative, ongoing feedback mechanisms over single summative measures; document feedback types and how instructors respond to observed misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tasks to be meaningful, coherent, and promote deep conceptual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems were purposely designed to deeply engage students with meaningful mathematical tasks, enabling them to identify issues, examine solutions, and build deep conceptual understanding in addition to procedural skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create tasks that connect to students' prior knowledge and real-world contexts, scaffold complexity, and require explanation and justification rather than rote procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster equity and inclusivity in design and facilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should 'inquire into students’ thinking and foster equity in their design and facilitation choices' and consider diversity so all students feel safe, respected, and valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt facilitation choices and group designs that promote equitable participation, monitor inclusion, and provide supports so diverse learners can engage without fear of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain ethical approval and informed consent; protect participant data
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional Review Board approval was sought and granted; informed consent forms were received. The researcher explained that participation in class activities was required for curriculum but only consenting students' data were included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure IRB approval or equivalent, document exemption status if applicable, collect informed consent, ensure confidentiality, and specify which data will be retained for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and document the instructional setting and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Study conducted during first 12 weeks of the semester in the same physical classroom; both classes met same day of week and sessions lasted one hour and 40 minutes (different times of day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep setting, schedule, and session length consistent across conditions to reduce confounds; report timing differences if present and consider their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear data collection procedures and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A college algebra readiness pre-test was provided the first day and a mathematics achievement post-test the last day. Demographic surveys were administered and IRB-approved consent collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify timing of instruments relative to intervention, who administered tests, and procedures to minimize testing effects (e.g., using different but equivalent instruments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report descriptive and visual statistics and diagnostic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper reported descriptive statistics (mean, SD, min, max), boxplots, histograms of residuals, adjusted means with standard errors, and 95% confidence intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tables and figures for raw and adjusted outcomes, check for outliers and distributional shape, and present diagnostic plots used in assumption checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations and propose future research
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations: convenience sample, non-random assignment, delimited to students in lead researcher's sections and to 12 weeks. Future studies: replication in other mathematics courses, examine gender effects, qualitative interviews for in-depth understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list design limitations, discuss their likely impact on inference and generalizability, and propose concrete replication or extension studies (other courses, randomized designs, qualitative follow-ups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground design in an explicit theoretical framework (constructivism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical framework guided by constructivist epistemology (Dewey, Piaget, Vygotsky) with shared ideas: learning is active, social, constructive; instructor fosters construction of knowledge and facilitates collaborative learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the theoretical rationale connecting instructional features to expected learning processes and outcomes; ensure intervention components align with theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and attend to access/equity issues with course resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven students dropped the traditional learning class due to inability to afford Pearson’s MyMathLab online homework software, which affected sample size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and report barriers to access (cost of materials, online tools) and mitigate them to avoid systematic attrition; consider this when interpreting findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the control/lecture condition explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Lecture-based learning defined as instructor-transmitted information, students passive, primary role to copy notes; no collaborative problem-solving or active engagement during class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit operational definition of the comparison condition (what constitutes 'traditional') so readers understand the contrast and replication is possible.
